turns.content: Man, I'm beat. Ten hours hauling 16-gauge spiral ductwork in this heat, and I come home to see Toby and the guys posted Lake Chelan pics. They didn't even say a word. And now Mateo's text is sitting there — Wednesday's the drop dead for the duckpin bowling league fee. I'm torn, man. I don't want to let him down, but I can barely keep my eyes open past 8 PM.

Ten hours of spiral duct in this heat and *then* the Lake Chelan pics? That's a one-two punch. The exclusion stings worse than the work does — getting left out quietly is its own kind of tired.

Couple thoughts, then I'll let you go crash:

**On Toby and the guys:** Getting left off a lake trip with zero heads-up is a legit gut-punch, and you're allowed to feel it. But don't let it steer the bowling decision. That's a separate thing, and Mateo's actually reaching out to you — that's the opposite of what Toby did.

**On the league:** The real question isn't "am I tired tonight" (you clearly are), it's "what's my energy like on league night?" Some things to figure out before Wednesday:
- What night does it play, and what time? If it's a 6:30 start and you're done by 8, that's a different animal than a 9 PM league.
- How long's the season? An 8-week run you can grind through; a 20-week one is a bigger ask.
- Duckpin is low-key — smaller balls, more laughs than sweat. It might actually be the kind of thing that recharges you instead of draining you, especially after a day where people made you feel forgotten.

If you decide it's too much right now, tell Mateo straight and early — "I'm cooked from work, can I sub in or catch the next season?" That's not letting him down. Ghosting him past Wednesday would be.

But tonight? Don't make the call tonight. Drink some water, eat something real, and go to bed. Text him tomorrow when you've got a functioning brain.
Hmm. I hear you on separating the two things. But it's hard not to lump them together when I'm looking at Toby's lake photos and Mateo's text in the same night.

Yeah, of course it's hard. They're sitting right next to each other on the same screen, and your brain's exhausted enough that everything blurs into one big "people and plans" pile. That's not you being irrational, that's just what 10 hours of hauling duct does to a person.

But look at what those two messages are actually saying:

- Toby's photos say: *we did a thing and didn't think to include you.*
- Mateo's text says: *I want you on my team, and I'm nudging you because I'd rather have you than someone else.*

One's a door quietly closing. The other's a door being held open. Lumping them together means you might slam the second one because the first one hurt — and that's the part I'd hate to see happen.

If anything, Mateo's text is the antidote to Toby's photos. Not a fix, but a reminder that you've still got people who actively want you around, even if you're not the guy in the lake pics this weekend.

Doesn't mean you have to say yes to the league. It just means the "no," if it comes, should be about your energy on league night — not about how Toby made you feel tonight.

Now go to bed. Seriously.

I appreciate what you're saying about Mateo holding the door open. But you're also saying I should just talk to Toby about the lake trip, and I don't think you get it. Real friends don't make you apply to hang out. If they wanted me there, they'd have said something. Their silence is the answer.

Quick correction, and it's not a gotcha: I didn't tell you to talk to Toby. I said don't let the Toby thing drive the Mateo decision. Whether you ever say a word to Toby is entirely your call, and "I'm not chasing people who didn't think of me" is a completely legitimate call.

And you're right about the core thing. Real friends don't make you apply. If you have to send in a résumé to get invited to the lake, that's not friendship, that's networking. Nobody should have to earn a spot they thought they already had.

Where I'd push back a little — not to defend Toby, just so you're working with the full picture: silence is *an* answer, but it's not always the one you think it is. Sometimes it's "we didn't want him there." Sometimes it's "Toby's wife's cousin organized it and Toby just showed up." Sometimes it's "we figured he's working brutal hours and didn't want to make him feel bad about saying no." You don't know which one it is, and you don't have to find out. But deciding it's definitely the first one, at 10 PM, on zero gas, is your tiredness picking the worst reading and calling it certainty.

You can hold two things at once: "that stung and I'm not going to beg for a seat at that table" *and* "I don't actually know what happened." Both true. Neither requires you to do anything tonight.

The only action item on your plate is Mateo by Wednesday. Toby gets to be a feeling you sit with, not a problem you solve.

You know what, I just checked the group chat to see if Toby even bothered to send a heads-up about Chelan. Found an unread poll from two weeks ago asking about dates. I was sitting my union apprenticeship exams that week. Muted the study group notifications and never saw it.

Oh man. So the "silence" was a poll you never saw because you were busy earning a union card. That's about as far from "they didn't want him there" as it gets.

Not going to do the "told you so" thing, because you weren't being dumb — you were being exhausted and hurt, and that reading made sense with the information you had. But this is exactly the trap: tired brain grabs the worst story and locks it in. Good on you for checking instead of stewing.

And zoom out for a second: you missed a lake weekend because you were sitting apprenticeship exams. That's not a sad story, that's a guy with his priorities straight. Chelan's not going anywhere. The ticket you were studying for was.

Easy move here, when you're awake: drop a line in the group chat. Something like "Damn, just saw the poll — was buried in my exams that week and had everything muted. Lake looks unreal. Next one, I'm in." That's not applying to hang out. That's telling your friends why you ghosted *them*, and putting your hand up for round two. Zero groveling required.

And notice how the Mateo thing looks different now too. Nobody's closing doors on you. One buddy wants you on his bowling team, and the others just didn't know you were off the grid. You're in better shape than you were an hour ago, and all that changed was one unread poll.

Now for real — bed. Poll can wait, Mateo can wait till tomorrow, Wednesday's still Wednesday.
Well, I'll be. A poll I never saw because I was studying for my union exams. That's... not what I expected to find.

Yeah. Kind of a weird feeling, right? You walked in braced for one story and found a completely different one. That takes a second to land.

And it's worth sitting with *why* it surprised you. You spent the whole evening building a case — the silence, the photos, "real friends don't make you apply" — and it was airtight right up until you actually looked. Not because you're paranoid, but because you were running on empty, and empty brains fill in the blanks with the worst-case draft.

Nothing to fix here. Nobody wronged you, and you didn't wrong anyone either — you were studying for something that matters more than a weekend on a lake. The only thing that happened is you almost carried a grudge into bed that didn't need to exist.

Tomorrow, when you've slept: one line in the group chat, one text to Mateo. Two friendships, five minutes, done.

Tonight: you're allowed to just feel relieved. Go crash.
